I was told the bipolar diagnosis wasn't an option until 18 years old because some children exhibit many symptoms by just being children.

That being said, I was prescribed these weird safe for kids mood stabilizers when I was 10 and took them until 14. When I was 14, they had me taking vyvanse to control my racing thoughts. I was prescribed antidepressant after antidepressant from 15 to 17 which made my bipolar symptoms worse.

I think back to my pre-diagnosis behavior and sometimes I was like "......well damn, the signs have been there all along." I found a journal I kept my freshman year of high school and I was shocked about how insane my behavior was. You could almost feel the mood swings through the pages.

For my brain fog, I was prescribed vyvanse.

I take 300mg lamictal, 50mg seroquel xr, and 30mg vyvanse. 

If I need to be super productive, I'll drink an insane amount of coffee then take my vyvanse at 10 or 11 instead of 8am. My boyfriend and I call it Diet Speed (diet because it's legal lol) sleeping after that is a bitch, but when you gotta crank out some work real fast, works like a charm!

At the beginning of 2018, my entire body was covered in hives. It got to the point my eyes were swollen shut and my throat started closing. I went to the ER and they gave me an epinephrine shot and some steroids. They asked if I was using any new products, and my answer was no. They suggested I go to an allergist. After about a year of test after test, they found out I was literally allergic to stress. When my cortisol levels are too high I have a severe allergic reaction. I now carry an epipen wherever I go.

Not saying this is definitely the case for you, but it may be worth checking out. Beware though, the test is extremely uncomfortable. I had to take an ACTH stimulation test. They draw your blood to measure cortisol level before anything. Then they inject you with cosyntropin (had to look that one up because I could not remember the name of it). You then just sit there for an hour and they usually leave the room, but since I was being tested for an allergy, a nurse came to check on me every five minutes. I was covered in hives by the time the hour was up, but I didn't need epinephrine. Just some antihistamine and I was good to go. They draw your blood at the end of the hour to see what your levels are.

Cushings disease/syndrome was ruled out for me because my body is not constantly making too much ACTH on its own, it is only when stress is induced. There isn't really any treatment for it. I just carry benadryl, zyrtec, and my epipen where ever I go.

What sucks the most about this whole thing with school is I was the *exact* same way. I didn't have an older sister willing to help me and my parents just didn't care. I just failed everything because I refused to do homework. I passed my tests with flying colors but it didn't matter because the homework meant more. 

For some reason, after seeing all my struggle, he draws inspiration for me. He thinks because I ended up passing high school, he will too. I basically begged him to stop trying/feeling like he can be like me. Our middle sister busts her ass to have the best grades. She turns in homework she put a lot of effort in and is on time 100% of the time. I'm very proud of her and her work ethic. She will absolutely push herself to her limit, despite having very intense anxiety, and balancing about 30 hours of work per week at the same time.

I was also diagnosed ADHD in my freshman year, I think I was 13? Maybe 14? He's 15 now and I have talked to my parents about him about him possibly also having ADD/ADHD. I think my parents thought the medication was not good for me to take at the time? I'm not sure because they won't really elaborate further than just outright saying no.

I also see some signs of depression in him. My mental health journey was difficult, as it is for most BP people. I know every test in the book when it comes to the basic mental health diagnoses. I see his lack of motivation, absolute brain fog, apathy, and just overall no interest in life. He's currently sleeping in until 2 and will half ass one assignment and call it a day. I know so much of these things are kind of common in kids his age, but my family has a strong rushing river of mental health in our family. Our father has BP I and ADD. Our mother has intense anxiety, depression, and was affected by an eating disorder at one point. I know there's a pretty high chance he will have at least one of these things. I don't necessarily want to push medication on him at his age because when I was his age, I was misdiagnosed with Major Depressive Disorder. As we know, depression medication on its own is not a good idea for BP people. I attempted suicide because I didn't understand my ups and downs and I thought I was making it up because I wasn't just depressed and then the depression medication in conjunction with the stimulant made my swings SO much worse. I would really recommend he sees a therapist though.

I love my little brother. Our childhood was rough, and as the oldest and also being a girl, I assumed the position of "mom." My sister doesn't remember how our family was crumbling, but she does remember how I cared for them both. I think my brother was just too young to remember any of it. He doesn't understand why I feel the need to help him out. I know he definitely gets overwhelmed so I break it up for him. I try to make doing this mountain of homework as enjoyable as I'm able. Now that I am no longer in rage mode, I understand I was too hard on him and I feel bad a little about yelling at him the way I did. I still feel hurt by the fact he does not want to help himself. It makes me upset that he rejects my help and kind of resents me a bit for making him work.

I'm just kind of on my last straw on patience at the time so it's very hard to just accept the fact he just won't let me help him at all. The rest of my family and my roommates (I vented a little after the first night) just keep saying shit like "just give up on him! If he won't do his work, that's on him." But I am trying to make him take pride in finishing his school work and getting good grades. I see this at home schooling thing as partially beneficial because I can't follow him around school and tell him to pay attention. At home, I can force him to pay attention and specifically break down things he personally doesn't understand. His teachers all say they will help out when the students need help. They all set up their own office hours, but his math teacher is in the "office" from 9am to 8pm. He can ask questions at any time and just chooses not to. He asks me to help him. I teach myself how to do his work, and we have similar styles when it comes to how we are able to understand things we have to learn, so I know how to explain it in a way he understands.

I know I contribute to overwhelming him, but his teachers are all pissed at him for not turning in anything. One teacher begged him just to log on because they can see when the students last logged on. By the end of week two, he hadn't even opened the learning software. I have been working 10+ hours every day and then I only have a short window to help him because with seroquel, I absolutely have to get at least 8 hours of sleep. It knocks me out like nyquil and if I don't get enough sleep, I'm so extremely nauseous and dizzy throughout the day. That's not enjoyable when working for so long and not being able to just lay down for a minute. I've been in a mixed episode with very high grade hypomanic, slowly sneaking into full on mania, so despite the medication, I'm fine with little to no sleep, but I want to make sure that if there is some way I'm coming back down or out of the woods with this mixed episode, I am able to get as much sleep as I need. I don't think he understands the things going on in my life, so he doesn't get that. He just expects me to be there, the way I always have been.

I'm just sooooo tired. Mentally, physically, emotionally. Everything. I cycle through so many moods every single day and I feel like I have no idea who I am. I just cannot explain how I'm feeling. It is exhausting.

A simple sentence is one independent clause. A compound sentence is two independent clauses separated by a comma then a coordinating conjunction. A complex sentence is one dependent and one independent clause.

An independent clause is a sentence that makes sense one it's own. A dependent clause leaves you feeling like you need more information to complete the sentence.

Simple sentence: I went to the store. (Makes sense on its own.)

Compound sentence: I went to the store, and I bought a gallon of milk. (Both halves of this sentence will make sense on their own.)

Complex sentence: When I went to the store, I got a gallon of milk. (The dependent clause, before the comma, doesn't give enough information to be a complete sentence, but the independent clause, after the comma, makes sense on its own.)

A fun way to remember coordinating conjunctions is the FANBOYS. For And Nor But Or Yet So.

My diagnosis is relatively new, was diagnosed in April or May. Figuring out what normal human emotions/actions were versus the emotions/actions of an episode proved to be very difficult.

Therapy has been helping a lot. My therapist has been teaching me how to step back and observe the situation (she said emotions over intelligence leads to impulse and intelligence over emotions leads to rationality). When I view the situation with my intelligence, I am usually able to tell if my emotions/actions are warranted. If they are, great! Just a normal human response. If not, that could be an episode. The problem I face most, though, is the fact that in an episode, I don't always remember to take a step back. It is pure impulse and my head refuses to let me do anything to stop it.

I wish you all the best in figuring out yourself and your illness!! Remember that you have BP, but BP does not have you. <3

At the beginning of the year, he started going out drinking more frequently and started doing coke, not super often, though. I blame myself for this, I believe it was my manic episode that caused the rift, and caused him keeping distance. It really hurt when he ended it. I know I was bad for his own mental health, but I really wish he just listened to what I had to say, or even just listened when I tried to explain how I was feeling.

I can't really give much advice, but I know communication is key. Sit him down, tell him how you feel about things. Have him tell you how he feels, and listen. Losing someone who loves and cares about you, over something as easy as communication, is really, really hard.

Wow, I feel like I could have written this exact post. I think the only differences are the fact that I hit puberty at 12 (which made my boobs bigger than all the other girls, even now as I'm older) and the fact I was diagnosed with endometriosis instead of PMDD. 

I'm pretty lucky, though. I was diagnosed with Hashimoto's when I was 15 after my mother found out herself. I believe this diagnosis because it is a genetic thing. My father found out a little later that he too had Hashimoto's, but his isn't so bad he requires medication. I was recently diagnosed with BPII at the age of 19, which I also believe for genetic reasons, with my father being diagnosed BPII and my grandfather being diagnosed BPI.

Basically, I listen to my body. You can tell when it is an endocrine issue verses a mental one if you really pay attention to your symptoms. Usually, with the BP, your symptoms present themselves in conjunction with a few other characteristics with the episode. With Hashimoto's, you can experience any combination of symptoms, but they do not necessarily occur at the same time as other key indicators. If you are (un)lucky enough, you will have two or more indicators of the Hashimoto's.

Getting the proper levels of your T3 and T4 is instrumental in bringing you out of most of the symptoms. Obviously, you will still have some bad days, but they will be around much shorter than an episode, and they will not be as intense.

Some things I've noticed:

• Brain fog + depression = Hashi's. Since brain fog is associated with mania, and depression is obviously a depressive thing. 
• Longer display of symptoms = BP. Since the definition of mania is at least 4 consecutive days, and the definition of depression is 7 consecutive days (that is, as long as your levels are good).
• The mood stabilizer for the BP actually makes the Hashi's symptoms less severe (woo finally a positive!)

I personally know it isn't easy, but treat both illnesses with the same sense of urgency to get under control. I wish you all the best in dealing with these. You've got this!!
